# Chapter 7: Creating the Right Environment for Data-Aware Design

## Overview
This chapter examines three principles for establishing a data-aware design environment: shared company culture and values, hiring the right people, and implementing supportive processes. Successful data-driven design requires cultural buy-in at all organizational levels.

## Shared Culture and Data Literacy
One of the goals of designing with data is to avoid or diminish the necessity of "gut" decision making. Consequently, data-aware environments break hierarchical decision-making structures. The stereotype of management-led, top-down decision making based on hunches cannot flourish in a data-literate environment. Rather, company-wide data literacy that includes addressing well-formulated, carefully investigated questions invites discussion, challenge, and most importantly the potential to be wrong.

This data is best when collected using multiple techniques—not just A/B testing, but also ethnographic field research, field deployments of prototypes, surveys, lab studies, usability research. Such grounded and carefully gathered user data drives decisions, and is a less risky prospect than relying on hunches from individual executives working from a "gut feeling." The underlying principle: data is an effective way to resolve conflicts in decision making without relying on rank, hierarchy, or company politics.

**The HIPPO Problem**
A 2007 paper by Ron Kohavi, Randal Henne, and Dan Sommerfield, "Practical Guide to Controlled Experiments on the Web: Listen to Your Customers not to the HIPPO," introduced the acronym HIPPO: "Highest Paid Person's Opinion." This term names the problem of deferring to executive intuition over empirical evidence.

**Netflix Case Study**
Netflix exemplifies this approach. John Ciancutti, former VP of Product Engineering, and Patty McCord, former Chief Talent Officer, demonstrate how data literacy across all roles became a source of freedom and innovation. The practice of leveraging data was well established and universally accepted throughout the company. It may have started at the top with Reed Hastings and Neil Hunt (Netflix CEO and CPO) driving and believing in the value of leveraging data, but it was also embraced by everyone through management to the individual contributors on the team.

Patty McCord notes that having a mechanism to measure whether you are doing the right thing for your customers allows more people to have a voice in the development of the product. One of the reasons that embracing A/B testing can help to mitigate a top-down approach to problem solving is that everyone can learn from experimentation.

When Reed Hastings had strong product ideas, he submitted them to the same rigorous A/B testing as everyone else in the product team. On rare occasions when he dictated the exact way a product idea would work, he did this on "his test cell"—the experimental group in the test he was backing. This cell would be tested against other cells that were proposed by the product team. If it didn't win, then it didn't get launched. Having upper-level management hold themselves accountable to the same process as the individual teams reinforced the practice of subjecting ideas, prototypes, features, and flows to grounded review through experimentation, and to the possibility of "failing" as a positive outcome. This value was central to Netflix's view of how the company should work.

**Implementing Cultural Change**
If you are trying to shift into a data-aware framework, it will be critical to look at the way product and design decisions have been made to date. If these decisions were largely in the hands of one or two individuals, then it's worth taking the time to make sure those people can understand and recognize the value of bringing in user/customer data into the decision-making process because in the end, they may find that their weight is diminished—as is the "weight" of any individual opinion. This is a good point to check with yourself as well: are you also comfortable and willing to see how incorporating data will change the weight of your own opinion within the design and product development process?

## Hiring the Right People
Data-aware environments require hiring people who are comfortable with ambiguity, experimentation, and the possibility of being wrong. Netflix's success stemmed partly from hiring practices that prioritized intellectual honesty over deference to hierarchy.

## Implementing Supportive Processes
Processes must support experimentation at all levels. Netflix institutionalized A/B testing as a default step in product development, ensuring executive-proposed changes went through the same rigorous evaluation as any team proposal. The "test cell" mechanism ensured accountability while normalizing the practice of submitting all ideas to empirical review.

## Overview

This chapter examines three principles for establishing a data-aware design environment: shared company culture and values, hiring the right people, and implementing supportive processes. The chapter emphasizes that successful data-driven design requires cultural buy-in at all organizational levels, not just within design teams.

## Principle 1: Shared Company Culture and Values

### Depth: Communicating Across Levels

Data-driven design aims to reduce reliance on "gut" decision-making and can disrupt traditional hierarchical structures. A data-literate environment does not support management-led, top-down decision-making based on hunches. Company-wide data literacy—grounded in well-formulated, carefully investigated questions—invites discussion, challenge, and the possibility of being wrong.

Data should be collected through multiple techniques beyond A/B testing, including ethnographic field research, field deployments of prototypes, surveys, lab studies, and usability research. Grounded, carefully gathered user data drives decisions and is less risky than executive hunches.

The 2007 paper "Practical Guide to Controlled Experiments on the Web: Listen to Your Customers not to the HIPPO" by Ron Kohavi, Randal Henne, and Dan Sommerfield addressed how data resolves decision-making conflicts without relying on rank, hierarchy, or company politics.

**Case Study: Netflix**

John Ciancutti, former VP of Product Engineering at Netflix, described how data literacy across all roles became a source of freedom and innovation. Patty McCord, former Chief Talent Officer for over 12 years, noted that mechanisms to measure customer impact allow more people to have a voice in product development.

Netflix's data-driven success stemmed from the practice being universally accepted company-wide. While it started with CEO Reed Hastings and CPO Neil Hunt believing in data's value, the approach was embraced from management to individual contributors.

Patty McCord observed that at Netflix, unlike other companies where CEOs operate freely, even executives submit to data. Any employee—including executives—can become convinced they already know the answer. A/B testing mitigates top-down problem-solving because everyone learns from experimentation.

When Reed Hastings had strong product ideas, he submitted them to the same A/B testing rigor as the product team. On rare occasions when he dictated a specific implementation, he ran it on "his test cell"—the experimental group he was backing. This cell was tested against other cells proposed by the product team. If it didn't win, it didn't launch.

This accountability extended to leadership reinforced the practice of subjecting all ideas, prototypes, features, and flows to grounded review through experimentation and treating the possibility of "failing" as a positive outcome.

### Implementing Cultural Change

Organizations shifting to data-aware frameworks must examine how product and design decisions have been made previously. If decisions relied on one or two individuals, ensuring those people understand and value customer data in decision-making is critical—because their influence, like any individual opinion, will diminish.

Individuals should also examine their own comfort with data reducing the weight of their opinions within the design and product development process.
